query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (HEA) coating that is treated by advanced laser cladding to create a Cr‐enriched surface will exhibit superior resistance to tribo‐corrosion degradation under elevated temperature and frictional conditions compared to untreated HEA coatings or conventional structural alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory HEA (e.g., WVTaTiCr alloy coating) in its standard, as-deposited state.
generation.intervention: Application of an advanced laser cladding treatment designed to drive surface segregation and enrichment of chromium (and related elements) on the HEA coating.
generation.conditions: Exposure to elevated temperatures (approximately 450°C–650°C) combined with mechanical wear (simulated friction/contact) that induces simultaneous oxidative and corrosive stresses.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent Cr-rich oxide (passivation) layer on the alloy surface as a result of laser cladding-induced elemental redistribution.
generation.mechanism: The Cr-rich passivating layer acts as a self-healing barrier; it impedes oxygen and corrosive ion ingress and resists mechanical wear, thereby reducing both oxidation degradation and tribological damage under harsh service conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The laser-clad, Cr-enriched HEA coating will show a significantly lower corrosion rate, reduced wear rate, and improved overall structural stability compared to untreated HEA coatings or conventional alloys under identical high-temperature, frictional environments.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (wear rate, corrosion rate, and degradation behavior) of standard refractory HEA coatings or conventional duplex stainless steels without surface modification.
generation.boundary: The enhanced performance is anticipated within the tested temperature range (up to ~650°C) and controlled friction conditions; performance gains under temperatures or mechanical stresses significantly beyond these limits remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: While preliminary evidence supports improved oxidation and corrosion resistance via Cr enrichment, the exact quantitative improvement in tribo-corrosion resistance and long-term stability of the self-healing film under cycling mechanical stress require further experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings on a standardized steel substrate: one set receiving the advanced laser cladding treatment to induce Cr surface enrichment and the other set processed under identical conditions without the additional surface treatment. Subject both sets to simultaneous elevated temperature (e.g., 600°C) and controlled mechanical wear (via sliding or pin-on-disk tests) in an environment that also simulates corrosive conditions (e.g., saline solution atmosphere). Monitor the degradation process over a fixed exposure time.
measurements: Surface chemical composition and oxide layer formation (using XPS/EDS analysis)
Wear rate and debris generation (via mass loss measurements and surface profilometry)
Corrosion potential and corrosion rate (through electrochemical impedance spectroscopy or potentiodynamic polarization)
Microstructural analysis before and after exposure (using SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser-clad, Cr-enriched HEA does not exhibit statistically significant reductions in wear and corrosion rates, nor the formation of a continuous and self-healing Cr-rich oxide, compared to the untreated control under identical conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract WVTaTiCr x ( x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared on a 42-CrMo steel plate using laser cladding. The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe. decision.trend: Early HEA studies primarily focused on modifying alloy compositions and processing routes to achieve favorable phase stability, mechanical strength, and oxidation/corrosion resistance under high‐temperature conditions. For example, work on refractory HEAs processed by selective laser melting and laser cladding demonstrated that adjusting elements such as Cr can refine the microstructure and promote the formation of protective phases. Over time, researchers shifted from bulk alloy design toward engineering specific features—such as controlled precipitation and tailored dendritic structures—to enhance resistance to environmental degradation. However, although improvements in corrosion and high-temperature oxidation have been achieved, few efforts have directly addressed the combined mechanical wear (tribological factors) coupled with corrosion, leaving tribo‐corrosion resistance as a mostly open challenge.
decision.unsolved: The key challenge remains to design an alloy system that can sustain a robust, adherent, and self-healing surface under simultaneous high-temperature and frictional (tribo‐corrosion) conditions. In other words, while bulk properties and passivation have been individually optimized, an integrated approach that couples surface mechanical integrity (to resist wear) with chemical stability (to resist corrosion) is still lacking.
decision.lever: Optimized surface enrichment of Cr (and related elements) via advanced laser cladding treatment to promote the formation of a continuous, self‐healing Cr-rich passivating oxide layer
decision.why: Given the trend of using composition adjustments (e.g., varying Cr content) and advanced processing to enhance corrosion and oxidation resistance in HEAs, the next logical step is to engineer the alloy surface specifically. By tailoring the surface chemistry through controlled laser cladding, it becomes possible to create an adherent, protective passivation film that resists both wear and corrosion. This approach directly targets the unsolved challenge of coupling tribological durability with chemical stability under extreme operating conditions.
